title: Matthew emphasizes enduring commandments
observation: Matthew's Jesus denies abolishing the Law and associates doing and teaching commandments with standing in the kingdom.
alternateReading: Matthew's fulfilment language can refer to the arrival of the kingdom and a new authoritative interpretation rather than an unqualified requirement that every Torah rule binds all later Gentile followers.
limitation: This is Matthew's literary presentation of Jesus; the historical occasion and relation to later Gentile communities are reconstructed, not independently observed.

title: Galatians assigns the Law a changed role
observation: Paul describes the Law's custodial role as bounded by the coming of faith and strongly resists circumcision being imposed on Gentile Christ-followers.
alternateReading: The target may be Gentile entry into Abraham's promise rather than a universal declaration that Jews must abandon Torah observance.
limitation: The precise applicability of Paul's argument to Jewish observance remains debated; the Thiessen source was checked at abstract level only.

title: Paul also upholds and positively describes the Law
observation: Romans 3:31 rejects nullifying the Law; Romans 7:12 calls the commandment holy; Romans 13 and Galatians 5 connect love with the Law's fulfillment.
alternateReading: These affirmations need not imply that Paul requires all Gentiles to observe every Mosaic regulation; 'fulfill' and 'establish' require argument-specific interpretation.
limitation: A simple 'Jesus keeps Law; Paul rejects Law' thesis omits contrary Pauline passages.

title: Mark's food-purity passage has a contested reading
observation: Mark 7 reports a dispute about handwashing, tradition, and defilement. The Greek phrase in 7:19c has been taken as an explanatory gloss that Jesus declared all foods clean.
alternateReading: Logan Williams argues that the phrase belongs to Jesus' digestive explanation, relating the debate to ritual impurity rather than a repeal of prohibited animals.
limitation: Competing grammatical analyses and translation punctuation must be stated; Mark 7 cannot simply be equated with abolition of all food laws.

title: Acts 15 and Galatians 2 narrate the dispute differently
observation: Acts presents communal deliberation and a formal decision concerning Gentiles, while Paul describes a meeting focused on his Gentile gospel and a later public disagreement with Peter.
alternateReading: Some interpreters harmonize the meetings as different perspectives on the same event; others consider separate meetings or editorial shaping.
limitation: Acts is a later narrative; it should not be quoted as Paul's unmediated report. Historical identity and sequencing of the meetings are debated.

title: Different meanings of obligation may explain part of the tension
observation: The texts speak about continuity of scripture, how God's promises reach fulfillment, inclusion of Gentiles, and moral transformation; these are not necessarily identical questions.
alternateReading: Matthew's insistence on even minor commandments can still represent a genuine disagreement with claims that all followers are released from specific Torah obligations.
limitation: Romans 10:4 uses telos, whose interpretation as end, goal or culmination varies. A reconciled reading is a hypothesis, not proof that there is no theological tension.
